name: Niri
summary: A scrollable-tiling Wayland compositor that keeps windows in a horizontally arranged layout, maps input and IPC actions into compositor state, and composes output resources through Smithay-based protocol handling.

features.name: Smithay-backed Wayland protocol boundary
features.description: Niri implements a Wayland compositor using Smithay protocol and backend abstractions, accepting client surfaces and coordinating protocol requests with compositor-owned layout, focus, and rendering state.
benefits: Reuses typed protocol and backend primitives while retaining compositor policy
Provides a clear client-to-compositor resource boundary
costs: Protocol behavior is constrained by Wayland and Smithay lifecycle contracts
A compositor process failure affects the session

features.name: Scrollable column layout
features.description: Niri arranges windows in columns along a scrollable workspace strip rather than requiring every window to fit a fixed virtual desktop; column widths, window placement, focus, and scrolling are compositor state.
benefits: Preserves usable window sizes as the workspace grows horizontally
Makes scrolling and column manipulation first-class layout operations
costs: Layout navigation differs from fixed-grid tiling expectations
Scroll position and column geometry add state to focus and output changes

features.name: Input and IPC state control
features.description: Niri maps keyboard and pointer input, configuration keybinds, and its IPC interface into actions over compositor state such as focus, movement, workspace selection, layout changes, and output management.
benefits: Exposes both interactive and programmatic control paths over one state model
Allows status bars and automation to observe or request compositor actions
costs: Concurrent input and IPC actions require deterministic ordering
The IPC surface adds a compatibility and authorization boundary to the session

features.name: Output and surface resource lifecycle
features.description: Niri tracks outputs, workspaces, columns, windows, and Wayland surfaces as resources whose geometry, visibility, focus, and rendering state are updated as clients and monitors appear or disappear.
benefits: Makes monitor hotplug and surface lifecycle part of the compositor state model
Supports output-specific scale, transform, and workspace placement
costs: Hotplug and surface destruction require coordinated geometry and focus updates
Backend or rendering resource failures can remove an output without removing all logical layout state

features.name: Transactional render and failure boundary
features.description: Niri applies layout and rendering updates across compositor state and output frames; protocol, client, backend, or framebuffer failures can reject part of an update or remove a resource while the remaining logical state continues under compositor policy.
benefits: Separates logical layout state from individual client and output resources
Provides explicit places to reason about rejected requests and unavailable rendering paths
costs: Failure recovery depends on backend and resource ownership details
The fixed revision does not prove transparent recovery for every rendering failure

mathematical_views.question: How do columns, windows, focus, scroll position, and workspace membership change under input, IPC, and client events?
assumptions: Columns form an ordered sequence with window stacks
Focus and scroll position are explicit state
Rendering geometry is derived from layout state

mathematical_views.question: Which compositor, output, workspace, window, surface, and backend resources own or reference one another?
assumptions: Ownership edges are modeled separately from protocol requests
The graph does not claim isolation beyond the documented protocol boundary

mathematical_views.question: Which logical layout states remain reachable after a rejected action, client disconnect, output loss, or render failure?
assumptions: Actions can be accepted, rejected, or partially reflected in resources
Client and backend failures have distinct transitions
This is a candidate model rather than a formal recovery proof

benefits: Typed protocol/backend foundations reduce duplicated compositor plumbing
costs: Policy and lifecycle behavior remain coupled to protocol and backend contracts

benefits: Windows retain width as the workspace expands
costs: Scrolling introduces additional focus and geometry state

benefits: Interactive and automation controls share one action model
costs: IPC ordering and compatibility become part of session correctness

benefits: Logical workspaces can outlive individual output resources
costs: Hotplug and destruction paths require coordinated state updates

benefits: Resource failures can be reasoned about separately from layout intent
costs: Partial update and backend failure behavior is difficult to observe
